q: Is the paper's central 'open pan-genome' claim (growth exponent γ = 0.162) an artifact of n = 19 genomes rather than a true species property, and at what n does the T. pyogenes pan-genome close (if it closes)?
basis: The authors themselves flag n = 19 as a limiting factor (§4: 'the number of genomes used in our study is limited to 19, which may be a limiting factor in true estimation of genome openness'), and explicitly cite Chan et al. 2015 who reversed a prior 'open' verdict on A. baumannii when scaling from 16 to 249 genomes. Our replication independently obtained γ = 0.247 with Roary — 52% higher than the paper — meaning the two runs disagree on the *magnitude* of openness while both nominally agreeing on the sign (γ > 0). Neither run tested convergence behavior. As of 2026, the number of publicly available complete or high-quality-draft T. pyogenes genomes (NCBI Assembly, GenBank, ENA, PATRIC/BV-BRC) is materially larger than the 19-genome snapshot the paper used; a rigorous n-scaling curve of γ has never been published for this species.
next_steps: (1) Pull every T. pyogenes genome from NCBI Assembly + BV-BRC + GTDB (target n ≥ 100 as of pull date) and QC-filter by CheckM completeness ≥ 95%, contamination ≤ 5%. (2) Run BOTH Roary AND PPanGGOLiN AND panaroo on identical input to separate tool-effect from n-effect. (3) Compute γ (Heaps' law fit) as a function of n using random subsamples n ∈ {19, 30, 50, 75, 100, ...} with ≥ 100 bootstraps at each n. (4) Report γ(n) with 95% CI; a true 'open' species should have γ that plateaus above 0; an artifact-of-small-n would show γ dropping toward zero. (5) Repeat stratified by host animal to test whether openness is a host-adaptation signal or a species-wide one.

q: Which specific fimbrial subunit CDS in T. pyogenes correspond to the paper's labels fimA, fimC, fimE, fimJ, and does the species actually carry four distinct paralogous fim subunits (as the paper implies), or is the four-way naming a legacy artifact carried over from Corynebacterium/Actinomyces literature?
basis: The paper labels four fimbrial-subunit CDS as fimA/C/E/J without providing NCBI reference accessions, and cites Bisinotto et al. 2016 (paper ref [13]) for the naming. Our replication located four candidate fimbrial-subunit CDS in the TP6375 Prokka annotation (CAOFJOCJ_00612, 01327, 01649, 01778) but Prokka itself does not assign the species-specific fim names, and no public sequence-to-name mapping exists. Our BLAST panel found fimA in 12/19 and fimE in only 2/19 (vs. paper's 19/19 for both) using our best-guess reference selection — a discrepancy so large it almost certainly reflects a reference-choice error, not a biological one. The literature on T. pyogenes fimbriae is dominated by 2–3 groups reusing each other's labels without a canonical accession registry.
next_steps: (1) Obtain Bisinotto et al. 2016 (JDS) and any earlier Jost & Billington papers that established the fim naming; extract the exact GenBank accessions or primer sequences used to define each subunit. (2) Build a curated T. pyogenes fim reference set with unambiguous accession → name mapping and deposit it (e.g., a small GitHub-hosted FASTA + JSON manifest). (3) Re-run BLASTN with the curated references against all 19 strains and any newer genomes from Q1. (4) Perform phylogenetic analysis of all four subunit paralogs to test whether they are truly paralogs (single ancestral duplication event within the species) or non-orthologous mislabeling. (5) Propose (and PR into Prokka/HAMAP) an authoritative gene-name mapping so downstream annotators stop guessing.

q: Are the paper's PHASTER-called 'incomplete' prophages in T. pyogenes bona fide prophage relics or false positives from short co-linear gene clusters (transposons, genomic-island cargo, or annotation artifacts)?
basis: The paper reports 30–31 prophages across 19 strains (range 1–4/strain) using PHASTER, but our free-tool substitute PhiSpy 5.0.10 detected only 7 total (range 0–1/strain) — a 4-fold difference. Both tools independently confirm the two INTACT prophages in TP6375 and TP1, so the disagreement is confined to PHASTER's 'incomplete' + 'questionable' categories. PHASTER's incomplete category is known in the literature to have a high false-positive rate for short prophage-gene clusters that co-localize with non-phage mobile elements. Neither the paper nor our replication tested the incomplete calls against orthogonal evidence (e.g., CheckV completeness, terminase presence, attL/attR flanking repeats, viral-vs-cellular gene-content Bayesian classifiers like Jaeger or geNomad).
next_steps: (1) Re-annotate all 19 strains with the modern gold-standard viral-detection stack: geNomad + CheckV + VirSorter2 + Jaeger, requiring ≥ 3-of-4 agreement to accept a prophage call. (2) For each PHASTER 'incomplete' call in the paper's Table S9, extract the ±20 kb flanking region and test for (a) integrase + terminase co-occurrence, (b) attL/attR direct repeats, (c) tRNA-adjacent integration site. (3) Cross-check against IslandViewer4 calls: if a PHASTER 'incomplete' overlaps an IV4 GI call at ≥ 50% but has no phage-specific hallmark, reclassify as GI. (4) Report a corrected prophage inventory with confidence tiers and estimate the false-positive rate of PHASTER 'incomplete' on this species. (5) Deposit the reannotated set as a benchmark dataset for T. pyogenes phage biology.

q: Does the 40-ARG resistome the paper reports translate into measurable phenotypic antimicrobial resistance in these strains, and are the strain-specific ARG differences (e.g. SH01/SH02/TP1 top-3 vs. the four zero-ARG strains) actually predictive of MIC-based susceptibility profiles?
basis: The paper is a pure genomic survey — it reports 40 ARGs via CARD/RGI but performs no phenotypic AST (antimicrobial-susceptibility testing) on any of the 19 strains. Our replication independently confirmed the strain-identity claims (top-3 = SH01, SH02, TP1; four zero-ARG strains = DSM20630, NCTC5224, Bu5, UFV1) but the free-tool ARG counts diverged (68 via abricate vs. 40 via paper's RGI-strict), primarily because abricate detects duplicate cassette copies (cmlA6/sul1/aadA on class-1 integrons) that RGI-strict collapses. Whether either count corresponds to a clinical breakpoint MIC in an actual disc-diffusion or broth-microdilution assay is unknown for the majority of these strains. The gap between genotypic ARG carriage and phenotypic resistance in Gram-positive veterinary isolates is a well-documented but chronically-underinvestigated problem.
next_steps: (1) Obtain the actual isolates (contacting the depositing institutions — several are ATCC/DSMZ/NCTC and thus purchasable). (2) Perform CLSI VET01-compliant broth microdilution against a T. pyogenes-relevant panel: tetracyclines, macrolides, lincosamides, β-lactams, aminoglycosides, phenicols, sulfonamides. (3) Correlate genotypic ARG presence (paper + our re-run) with phenotypic MICs; compute per-drug PPV/NPV of genotype→phenotype prediction. (4) For discordant cases (ARG present but susceptible, or ARG absent but resistant), sequence-verify the ARG (Sanger the tet(W) locus etc.) and check for premature stops, promoter mutations, or efflux-pump upregulation. (5) Report a T. pyogenes-specific genotype-to-phenotype rule set that veterinary clinical labs can actually use.

q: Does the paper's core-genome three-clade phylogenetic partition (Clade I/II domestic-ruminant, Clade III mixed) reflect true host-driven diversifying selection, or is it a founder/geographic-sampling artifact that would collapse under an expanded, host-balanced, geography-balanced sample?
basis: The paper reports three clades in the 19-strain core-genome FastTree phylogeny and claims host-association (Clades I+II = domestic large ruminants; Clade III = mixed). Our replication independently reproduced the three-clade structure with the same tool (FastTree from Roary core). BUT: the 19 strains are extremely unbalanced by geography (over-representation of Chinese and one Indian isolate, sparse European/African/Americas coverage) AND by host (heavy skew toward bovine mastitis isolates). The paper itself notes strains TP3/TP6375/TP4479/TP-2849 are ~100% identical (branch length ~0), suggesting they may be clonal descendants of a single source — inflating apparent clade-I 'coherence'. No dN/dS test, no core-genome recombination correction (ClonalFrameML/Gubbins), and no host-permutation p-value was reported. Without these, the host-association claim is descriptive rather than statistical.
next_steps: (1) Recruit a host-balanced sample: aim for ≥ 20 isolates each from bovine, porcine, ovine, and wildlife hosts across ≥ 4 continents (leveraging veterinary diagnostic labs and reference culture collections). (2) Build the phylogeny with Gubbins/ClonalFrameML to remove recombinant regions before tree inference. (3) Compute the Fritz–Purvis D statistic (or Pagel's λ) for host-clustering on the tree — this gives a formal p-value against the null of random host distribution. (4) Perform per-gene dN/dS scans (HyPhy BUSTED / aBSREL) focused on virulence and surface-protein genes to identify host-adaptation candidates. (5) If host-association holds, use ancestral-state reconstruction to test whether host jumps are rare (one-way commitment) or promiscuous (frequent switching), which has direct implications for zoonotic-risk modeling.
